Q: List all packages installed with winget A:

As of v1.28.220 of winget, there is currently no way to get this information, at least not using winget itself: Tip of the hat to Demitrius Nelon

  • Demitrius' GitHub issue #1155 proposes several future enhancements to winget list, though they don't appear to address the specific use case at hand either.

  • While Windows Package Manager does keep track of what packages were installed with it locally, via winget.exe or presumably also via PowerShell's Install-WinGetPackage cmdlet (part of the Microsoft.WinGet.Client module), this information is currently an implementation detail that isn't accessible to end users.[1]

    • A conceivable but suboptimal workaround would be to create a wrapper around winget that maintains its own list of installed packages, as discussed in stemarcoh's answer. Obviously, this would only cover packages installed via the wrapper.

Note:

  • Fundamentally, winget list lists all installed applications (as also shown interactively in Control Panel\Programs\Programs and Features), irrespective of how they were installed and including applications that cannot be installed with winget.

  • The best you can do is to filter the output so as to list only those locally installed packages that can be installed with winget, though not necessarily were:

    # List only packages that are installable via winget
(winget list) -match '\S$'

    • Notably, entries listing msstore as the source may have been installed interactively.

    • The above command relies on the fact that installed packages / applications not matching a configured Windows Package Manager source have a blank source column value.

      • The above-linked GitHub issue links to a proposal to support this functionality with a dedicated --no-source option in the future: GitHub issue #1488

    • Conversely, if you want to limit output to those packages available from a given source, say the Windows Package Manager Community Repository, identified as source winget:

      (winget list) -match ' winget$'
      • Note that while there is a dedicated -s / --source option that should provide this functionality, it currently doesn't work: see GitHub issue #4236.

[1] Demitrius notes, "WinGet does have a small sqlite database to track what it installed. It's used primarily for correlation with installed packages and the source last used or used at that point in time. That is an implementation detail of WinGet, so logically it's not really useful (other than for debugging scenarios)."

Q: How to perform the "uncollapsing" of a one row data frame or array to multiple rows in R A:

Haven't found the shorthand yet. This is outer way (a function I personally try to avoid):

x = unlist(collapsed) ## or as.numeric(collapsed) (faster? and unnamed)
m = outer(x, x, pmin)
m[upper.tri(m)] = NA

> m
   v1 v2 v3 v4 v5
v1  1 NA NA NA NA
v2  1  2 NA NA NA
v3  1  2  3 NA NA
v4  1  2  3  4 NA
v5  1  2  3  4  5

Skipped data.frame(m). It might be helpful to stay with a matrix.

Q: Where in the C standard does it specify the corresponding argument for %n in fscanf shall be a pointer to int or unsigned int A:

Many of the other conversion specifiers state one of the following:

Unless a length modifier is specified, the corresponding argument shall be a pointer to int.

Unless a length modifier is specified, the corresponding argument shall be a pointer to unsigned int.

The fact that such as sentence is missing from the description of the n specifier is, as far as I can tell, a defect in the standard.

The statement in the standard about the n specifier

The corresponding argument shall be a pointer of a signed integer type.

is insufficient, because as correctly pointed out in the question, a long long int is also a "signed integer type".
